title: Bridal jewellery checklist: every piece an Indian bride needs
description: A head-to-toe bridal jewellery checklist for Indian brides, from maang tikka to bichhiya, plus the small extras people forget and what you can skip.
intro: Most Indian brides need jewellery for six zones: head, ears and nose, neck, arms, hands, and waist and feet. Which pieces you wear in each zone depends on your family and region, so treat this as a master list to tick or strike out, not a rulebook. Go through it two months before the wedding so nothing is bought in a last-minute rush.

sections.heading: Head and hair
paragraphs: This is where the bridal look begins, and it is also the zone that changes most between communities.

Plan the head pieces together with your hairstylist, because the hairstyle decides where a tikka sits and whether a passa can be anchored securely. A low bun needs a different setup from open curls, and heavy head jewellery needs a firm base of pins underneath.
list: Maang tikka: the classic centre-parting piece. Choose the drop length based on your forehead height.
Mathapatti or sheeshphool: a fuller head ornament with side chains, for brides who want more drama.
Passa or jhoomar: worn on one side of the head, popular in Muslim and Punjabi bridal looks.
Hair pins and a juda or bun ornament, especially if your dupatta will be draped low at the back.
Dupatta pins or brooches to hold heavy fabric in place without pulling your hair.

sections.heading: Ears and nose
paragraphs: Earrings are the piece you will see most in close-up photos, so give them real thought.
If your lobes are sensitive, practise wearing the main pair for a few hours in the weeks before the wedding. It is far better to discover discomfort at home than halfway through the pheras.
list: Main bridal earrings: jhumkas, chandbalis or long Kundan drops that match the necklace.
Ear chains or sahare, which take some of the weight off the lobe.
Nath: a large nose ring, often with a chain clipped to the hair. Clip-on versions exist if your nose is not pierced.
A spare lighter pair for the long hours after the main ceremony.

sections.heading: Neck
paragraphs: Many brides wear two necklaces: a choker close to the neck and a longer haar. Choose by your blouse neckline first. If your family follows the tradition, the mangalsutra is added during the ceremony itself, so leave room for it in your layering plan.
A matching bridal set saves effort here, because necklace, earrings and tikka are designed to sit together. Our [bridal jewellery](/women/bridal-jewellery) page shows how full sets come together.
list: Choker or short necklace
Long necklace or rani haar
Space reserved for the mangalsutra, if part of your ceremony

sections.heading: Arms, wrists and hands
paragraphs: This zone has the most regional variety. Punjabi brides usually wear a chooda gifted by the maternal side, Maharashtrian brides often wear green glass bangles, and Bengali brides traditionally wear red and white shakha pola. Check with your elders before buying anything here.
list: Bangles or chooda, plus kaleere if your family follows that custom
Kadas to frame the bangle stack
Bajuband or armlet for sleeveless or short-sleeve blouses
Haathphool: a ring joined to a bracelet by chains, which looks lovely against mehendi
One or two statement rings, kept light enough to remove for rituals

sections.heading: Waist and feet
paragraphs: These pieces are often skipped by brides in a lehenga, but they finish the look in full-length photos.
If your toes are not used to rings, ask for adjustable bichhiya so they can be loosened comfortably during the long hours of the ceremony.
list: Kamarbandh or waist belt, which also helps hold a saree drape in place
Payal or anklets
Bichhiya or toe rings, which in many North Indian families are put on during the wedding rituals

sections.heading: The small things people forget
paragraphs: These do not show in photos, but missing them causes the most stress on the day.
list: Extra earring backs and a few spare dori tie-strings for necklaces
Safety pins and bobby pins in a small pouch
A soft cloth and zip pouches to store each piece after you take it off
A potli or clutch for your phone, lipstick and a spare pair of earrings
Separate, lighter jewellery for mehendi, haldi, sangeet and reception

sections.heading: What you can safely skip
paragraphs: You do not need every item above. If your dupatta covers most of your head, a full mathapatti will barely be seen, so a tikka is enough. If you are wearing full sleeves, skip the bajuband. If your lehenga is very heavy at the waist, a kamarbandh may add bulk without adding beauty. A good rule is to pick three hero pieces, usually earrings, necklace and tikka, and keep everything else supportive and lighter. That keeps the look regal without making you feel weighed down by the third hour.

faq.q: What are the must-have pieces for an Indian bride?
faq.a: Most brides wear a maang tikka, earrings, at least one necklace, bangles and a ring. Everything else depends on family customs and your outfit.

faq.q: How early should I buy bridal jewellery?
faq.a: Shortlist around two months ahead and finalise once your outfit and blouse neckline are fixed, so the shapes match.

faq.q: Can I wear a clip-on nath at my wedding?
faq.a: Yes. Many brides without a nose piercing use clip-on or press-on naths. Do a trial to check it stays put through the ceremony.

faq.q: Do I need different jewellery for each function?
faq.a: Ideally yes, but you can reuse pieces cleverly. Lighter earrings and a simple necklace often work for mehendi and haldi both.
